title: Dutch intelligence services warn AI is making cyberattacks faster and easier
content:
Dutch intelligence services warn AI is making cyberattacks faster and easier
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to automate and streamline cyberattacks, according to Dutch intelligence services AIVD and MIVD and five other organizations. In an open letter, the organizations urge business leaders and other organizations to “take responsibility and prioritize cybersecurity.”
The open letter was also signed by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the National Coordinator for Counterterrorism and Security (NCTV), the police, the Public Prosecution Service and CIO Rijk, the central government’s ICT organization.
The organizations warn that AI is making cyber threats faster and lowering the barrier for more malicious actors to launch attacks. They also say AI allows vulnerabilities to be found and exploited more quickly, while existing weaknesses are being magnified.
The organizations are urging businesses and other institutions to strengthen their basic cybersecurity measures. They recommend keeping systems up to date, fixing vulnerabilities, closely monitoring IT networks and making sure executives understand the latest developments.
They also emphasize the importance of the “human factor.” The signatories therefore advise organizations to “invest in awareness, changes in behavior and culture, and report incidents to the authorities.”
Cybercriminals can use AI to create malware that steals or encrypts data and to generate phishing emails aimed at obtaining sensitive information, including passwords.
Cyberattacks can have serious consequences, particularly when large amounts of personal information such as names, addresses and passport details are stolen. However, the damage may not always be apparent right away. Corporate espionage, for example, can lead to problems only at a later stage.
Attackers do not necessarily need sophisticated AI systems to launch cyberattacks, the organizations warn. Commonly available AI models can already provide enough capabilities for malicious purposes. ChatGPT, Claude and Google Gemini are examples of such widely accessible tools. Their developers say they are taking steps to prevent abuse, but security incidents, including hacks, still occur regularly.
The organizations stress that cybersecurity should be a shared responsibility rather than something left solely to IT teams and security experts. “Improving our country’s digital resilience is a task for all of us, in both the public and private sectors,” they wrote.
Reporting by ANP

report.summary: Dutch intelligence agencies AIVD and MIVD, joined by five partners, warn that widely available AI tools are making cyberattacks faster, cheaper, and accessible to far less skilled criminals.
report.background: For years, sophisticated cyberattacks required specialist skills, custom tooling, and time. That barrier has been eroding with the rise of large language models and generative AI, which can draft fluent phishing text, translate campaigns into any language, and help write or debug malicious code. Dutch authorities have tracked this shift in successive annual threat assessments, but the new open letter marks a coordinated public intervention: intelligence (AIVD, MIVD), the National Cyber Security Centre, counterterrorism coordinator NCTV, police, prosecutors, and the government's own IT organization CIO Rijk are jointly telling boardrooms that cyber risk is now a governance issue, not just a technical one. The warning also lands against a backdrop of European regulation such as NIS2, which pushes cybersecurity accountability toward executives and requires faster incident reporting across critical sectors.
key_points: Seven Dutch organizations — including the AIVD, MIVD, NCSC, NCTV, police, Public Prosecution Service and CIO Rijk — signed a rare joint open letter urging business leaders to 'take responsibility and prioritize cybersecurity,' framing digital resilience as a shared public-private duty rather than an IT department problem.

The signatories stress that attackers do not need sophisticated or custom-built AI. Readily available commercial models such as ChatGPT, Claude and Google Gemini already offer enough capability for malicious use, even though their developers say they are actively working to prevent abuse.

AI accelerates the whole attack chain: it helps criminals find and exploit software vulnerabilities faster, automates malware creation for stealing or encrypting data, and mass-produces convincing phishing emails designed to harvest passwords and sensitive information.

The letter warns that AI magnifies existing weaknesses, meaning organizations with poor patching, unmonitored networks or outdated systems become easier targets — so basic hygiene is presented as the highest-value defense.

Beyond technical fixes, the signatories emphasize the 'human factor,' recommending investment in awareness, behavior and culture change, executive education on emerging threats, and prompt reporting of incidents to authorities.
Damage is not always immediate. Stolen personal data such as names, addresses and passport details can cause cascading harm, while corporate espionage may only surface months or years later.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the letter intensifies pressure on model providers to prove that abuse prevention, usage monitoring and safety evaluations actually work at scale, and it strengthens the case for regulation tying liability to foreseeable misuse. For developers, it signals that AI-assisted coding cuts both ways: the same models that speed up vulnerability discovery can accelerate patching, making secure-by-design practices and software supply-chain hygiene non-negotiable. For regular users, expect more convincing, personalized phishing and a higher chance of their data appearing in breaches, even from organizations they do not directly deal with. Security teams, meanwhile, face rising attack volume and will likely lean on AI-driven detection to keep pace.
report.tools: To follow up: MITRE ATT&CK for mapping attacker behavior, and OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications for AI-specific risks. For LLM red-teaming, see Microsoft's PyRIT and NVIDIA's Garak. Defensive staples include Wazuh, Zeek and Suricata for monitoring, GoPhish for phishing simulations, and Microsoft Security Copilot for AI-assisted triage. On the policy side, track NCSC-NL advisories, the EU's NIS2 requirements, and the abuse policies and transparency reports from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
